Sure. Forgive the length, but there's a fair bit to say. I think it is interesting though. To preface it, it's been weeks, and I don't feel like going back to find the original article, which went into greater depth on the Hebrew words themselves. I'll just try to recall the main points. Don't worry, I won't be quoting scripture.

To understand the significance of what these 50 'children' say to Elisha, we require the context of 1 Kings the foregoing parts of 2 Kings prior to 2:23-24. Elisha's forerunner, Elijah, has appeared in Palestine as a figure that very much prefigured Jesus. He is a prophet travelling across Israel during a dark period of the nation's history, performing miracles, and confronting evil kings. There is a tremendous amount of material out there about the similarities between Elijah and Christ.

The two main pagan kings that Elijah challenges are Ahab and Ahaziah, and the miracles that were involved in these confrontations (which served to prove the power of Elijah's God) made him famous throughout Palestine. At a climactic point in the story, Ahab challenged Elijah to a 'God-off' on the top of Mt. Carmel, consisting of a prayer race to see whose God could produce miraculous fire first. This did no less than pit Baal against YHWH. Ahab and his priests try for several hours to no avail, while Elijah waits patiently. Then, just to make his demonstration more profound, Elijah stands and goes to soak his sacrifice in water first. He prays. God sends a brilliant fire to destroy the sacrifice of Elijah.

This angers all of the Baal-worshippers in Israel, and as Elijah and Elisha (who God called to be Elijah's successor) are moving through Jordan they are attacked by a group of 50 of king Ahaziah's mercenaries. God sends down the same fire as before to destroy the group of 50 mercenaries. This proselytizing journey takes place over a swath of time, and after a while it is noticeably taking a toll on Elijah, so that he knew his time was coming and that the two would be separated. He asks Elisha - who would take up his mantle - "What may I do for you before I am taken away from you?"

At that point Elijah is supposed to have been whisked up in a whirlwind/chariot of fire. A lot of people take it that he went to Heaven, but it isn't clear. The sons of the prophets all say, "The spirit of Elijah now rests on Elisha." This just means: Elisha is anointed and we're following him now.

Word spreads, gaining Elisha the same reputation for power and infamy among the Baal-worshippers. By the time we get to the story about Elisha going up to Bethel, the king Joram (I think) would have known Elisha was coming. At this point, Elisha would have had a reputation similar to what the Gospels said about Christ. This is where the language issues get interesting.

So Elisha is walking the path into Bethel, and he is confronted at the outskirts of the city by a group of 50 'children'. The Hebrew term which we translate as 'children' doesn't connote the same thing as the English term does; the difference has everything to do with Hebrew culture and religion. In English, 'children' is simply a signifier of age (perhaps of size, and innocence), but in Hebrew it is a term that refers to a situation of maturation and social-acceptance across a wider age-range. For the Hebrews, you were not a man until you had married and gave a woman children (it's important to remember that nothing in their culture was not religious). So the Hebrew term that we translate in KJV as 'children' actually refers to someone between the ages of 12-30 who is immature, who is not yet a man or has not yet assumed a manly place in the social hierarchy via accepting certain responsibilities.

Now, this is where it is interesting. Just like the term 'boy' in English can be used in different ways, so too can this Hebrew word. A Hebrew would not think of calling a 12-yr-old a child as very derogatory, but as a male ascends in years (say, into his late teens and definitely by his 20s and 30s), if he he had not started a family, he would have become something like we call a delinquent today - someone who spends their time like a gang member or fraternity brother in groups of other men that are generally doing nothing productive. But, the stakes in this story are even higher than this.

To offer one more linguistic example where the English term 'boys' demonstrates the same kind of varied usage, think of the song The Boys Are Back In Town. Nobody thinks 'boys' in this song indicates young boys. There is the connotation where the 'boys being back' means we're about to tear it up: sure we're grown ups, but these are 'my boys' and we're going to go cause some trouble because we haven't gotten together in a while. The same idea is communicated by the phrase 'frat boy'. Nobody thinks this means an actual boy, but a man who is not yet a man, who is generally cocky and not up to much good.

We'd still be missing context if we forget what had been taking place during Elijah's travels, and this huge buildup of tension between the pagans and the YHWH-worshipping Jews. Before Elijah had left the picture, he'd gone into a city and met with the pagan king Ahaziah, whispered in his ear that his rulership would be ending soon, and Ahaziah died within the year. Everyone would have known about this, so later as Elisha is approaching the paganized town Bethel, it would have been something like Trump's biggest supporter showing up to Portland, Oregon, intent on waltzing into town hall just after he'd been to California and murdered Gavin Newsom. We cannot forget how seriously these people took spiritual warfare, and how they would have interpreted these events.

So as Elisha is coming down the path, a group of young men (who knew that he was coming) are going to confront him before he can enter. Do we think this means a bunch of 8 yr-olds? I highly doubt it. It is probably something closer to what we'd take Antifa to be today: a group of delinquents that haven't assumed a normal, mature lifestyle (hence their being 'children' to he Hebrews, despite being in their 20s).

Another mistake is that the gang was mocking him simply for being bald, having a bit of fun just heckling. The closest translation we have to the original Hebrew for the gang's words is: 'go on up, baldhead'. This was actually a death threat. As I said before, everyone in this region was aware of the situation with Elisha's predecessor, and there existed no less than a state of spiritual warfare at this time. When the gang says to Elisha, 'go on up', they are referencing Elijah being caught up in the fiery chariot that symbolized him going to Heaven. So this gang was saying no less than, 'go to heaven', or subtly indicating, 'If you attempt to enter here, you'll be going on up (you'll die)".

Elisha turns back on the path and curses the group, and two 'she bears' attack the gang blocking the path. Now, we can take this bear thing literally, or figuratively. If we take it literally, then we'd be talking about the brown bears of ancient Palestine, today called a Syrian brown bear, which are relatively small. We might think that the attack resulted in injuries, but the effect had more to do with disrupting the group, causing them to flee so that Elisha could pass. (pic of Syrian brown bear below)

https://files.catbox.moe/joac32.jpg

Alternatively, I have wondered if this wasn't a bit of humor. I can't ignore that they were called 'she' bears. This could have referred to the sex of the bears, but I find that an extremely odd detail to specify in a Biblical text, especially given the brevity of detail already in these stories. So I've considered that this might be a humorous metaphor for women in the town, perhaps some kind of regulator, but more likely mothers of some of these young men. It sounds funny, but again, if we consider the foreknowledge everyone in Bethel had of Elisha's coming and how serious this was, then we might picture this being like a group of 19 yr-old Antifa getting broken up and dispersed by a group of older women (perhaps their own mothers). If these were some mean bitches, it might have occurred to the author to think, "these fucking she bears came and busted them up". I'm speculating, of course - and simply acknowledging that even ancient authors probably found humorous ways to create literary metaphor.

My point had less to do with the bears, and more to do with establishing that in this story, the stakes were a lot higher than they strike moderns like us. For one, the spiritual significance in their politics/economics was something we can hardly understand, that these people literally saw God as able to level the existing order and power structure by sending a man into your city. So the whole context of this story in which Elijah (and then Elisha) had been doing exactly this, means that this group of 'children' was not what we imagined. These were probably a gang of young men far closer to our modern example of Antifa. They didn't jeer at him for his bald head just to demoralize him on his way through. Instead, they were issuing a clear death threat with "go on up, baldhead", while connecting him with his predecessor, Elijah.

What language would it be in? Could it even contain metaphor, humour, literary devices? If not, would it not have to be the totally stoic, formal, literal "million-page-book" that ARM complains about God not having provided - something totally emotionless, devoid of soul, but which contained a page reference for every possible moral quandary?

Such an approach just runs contrary to the entire point God had in creating. So see higher truth through lower signs is the entire point; in a very real sense, the "million-page-book" would be constitutionally incapable of revealing what Scripture reveals, even though it would have used many more words. Christ only taught in parables to crowds for this very reason; not only can more be said, but more can be understood.

So if we do decide that relying on metaphor and literary device is better, this necessarily entails the use of a specific language situated within a specific people. God could then have provided a Bible for every people and every culture, or He could have chosen one among them all to provide this. Since He also chose to redeem humanity by Himself taking on human nature and sacrificing it (and Aquinas explains well the many very important things this choice allows God to indicate to us), then it can readily be seen how choosing one people to reveal His word to, as a pre-cursor to the Word Himself taking on human flesh, is the ideal choice; since Christ Himself had to come of one race, and not all races, likewise the Word that preceded Him was revealed to one race, and in fact this same race. In short, "it had to be some nation".

The history of the Jews, as we all know, is unique among all other nations - for good and for ill. We should find this unsurprising in the context of God have chosen them to receive His initial Word, and His Word Himself.

Finally, God understood the need for interpretation of His Word. It is recounted in the story of Phillip's encounter with the eunuch (Acts 8:29-35). Philip (a disciple) asks the eunuch, who is reading Scripture, is he understands it. The eunuch responds with incredulity: "How can I, unless you tell me what it means?" Philip then proceeds to provide exegesis. Philip, a disciple, is a priest, a representative of the Church. This passage does not mean that lay people lack reason or cannot speculate; it means that ultimately all speculation must defer to the authority of the Church, which Christ founded for the express purpose of providing proper exegesis, i.e. sound doctrine. Christ knew that the Church was necessary for this, and many other purposes (providing the sacraments not least of all). That's why He founded it. So we don't need to rely on RapGenius; we have the Church, and all its tradition.

I will also point out (although it may not be relevant in this case) that the translation of the Bible used is key. Different translations came into being for different reasons. The King James Version was written to be read in the court of King James; thus "being pleasing to the ear" was prioritized over being faithful to original meanings, or even making sense. If the King would have laughed at a bunch of pagans getting mauled by bears because they called Elisha bald, then that is all that matters. The only reasonably faithful English translation of Scripture is Douhay-Rheims. How does it report on this same event? Obviously the details won't change but the portrayal very well may, rendering the whole scene perhaps less absurd, and less dependent on background information like that which Chiro has provided to make sense of it. 2 Kings 2:23-25.
